name: Brain
description: A sophisticated organ comprising 86 billion neurons, orchestrating sensation, cognitive thought, motor action, and emotional homeostasis.

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Internal carotid & vertebral arteries (Circle of Willis)

keyFacts.label: Function
keyFacts.value: Cognition, movement, and vital autonomic control

medicalImportance: Susceptible to acute ischemic stroke and herniation; zero ischemic tolerance beyond a few minutes.
didYouKnow: The brain itself has no pain receptors; neurosurgeries can be performed while patients remain awake.

parts.name: Cerebral Cortex
parts.description: The convoluted 2-4 mm thick outer grey matter mantle of the cerebral hemispheres, divided by the longitudinal fissure and major sulci into frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes.
parts.function: Executive cognitive control, voluntary motor initiation (primary motor cortex M1), somatosensory processing (S1), language comprehension (Wernicke) and production (Broca), and conscious perception.
connections: Interhemispheric communication via ~200 million axonal fibers of the Corpus Callosum
Receives thalamocortical sensory projections from thalamic relay nuclei
Sends corticospinal and corticobulbar projection fibers through the internal capsule
Supplied by Circle of Willis: Anterior, Middle, and Posterior Cerebral Arteries
parts.clinicalNote: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) ischemic stroke causes contralateral hemiparesis and hemianesthesia (face/arm > leg) plus aphasia (dominant hemisphere). Convolutions maximize surface area (~2500 cm2).
keyFeatures: Houses ~16 billion cortical neurons arranged in six distinct horizontal laminae
Consumes 20% of total body resting glucose and oxygen despite weighing only 2% of body mass
Frontal prefrontal cortex drives executive decision-making and personality
Primary visual cortex (V1) situated along the banks of the calcarine sulcus
parts.histology: Six-layered neocortex (molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal with Betz cells, multiform) supported by astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia.

parts.name: Cerebellum
parts.description: Located in the posterior cranial fossa inferior to the tentorium cerebelli and dorsal to the pons and medulla. Features an extensively folded foliate cortex with central vermis and lateral hemispheres.
parts.function: Coordinates voluntary motor movements, precision, timing, postural equilibrium, and vestibulo-ocular reflexes through real-time motor error detection and procedural motor learning.
connections: Connected to brainstem via Superior, Middle, and Inferior Cerebellar Peduncles
Receives massive mossy fiber input from pontine nuclei carrying motor intent copies
Receives climbing fibers from inferior olivary nucleus signaling motor errors
Outputs via deep cerebellar nuclei (Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial)
parts.clinicalNote: Cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing), dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements), nystagmus, and scanning staccato speech.
keyFeatures: Contains over 50% of all neurons in the human brain packed into 10% of total brain volume
Famous for giant Purkinje cells possessing enormous planar dendritic arborizations
Functions as an offline motor coprocessor calibrating muscular trajectories
Vulnerable to chronic alcohol toxicity (vermis degeneration and cerebellar ataxia)
parts.histology: Three distinct cortical layers: outer synaptic molecular layer, middle monolayer of giant GABAergic Purkinje cells, and inner dense granule cell layer (tiniest and most numerous neurons in brain).

parts.name: Brainstem (Midbrain, Pons & Medulla)
parts.description: The stalk-like posterior structural core of the brain extending from the diencephalon down through the foramen magnum to merge continuously with the cervical spinal cord.
parts.function: Houses vital autonomic regulatory centers controlling respiration (dorsal/ventral respiratory groups), cardiovascular tone (vasomotor center), heart rate, and protective reflexes (coughing, vomiting, swallowing).
connections: Transmits all ascending somatosensory tracts (dorsal columns, spinothalamic)
Transmits all descending motor pathways (pyramidal corticospinal tracts decussating at medulla)
Houses cranial nerve nuclei III through XII
Contains the Reticular Activating System (RAS) maintaining cortical arousal and wakefulness
parts.clinicalNote: Uncal or tonsillar brain herniation compresses the brainstem, producing Cushing's triad (severe hypertension, bradycardia, irregular Cheyne-Stokes breathing) indicating impending fatal brainstem death.
keyFeatures: Anatomical crossroads: 90% of motor corticospinal fibers decussate at the medullary pyramids
Nucleus tractus solitarius receives all visceral sensory baroreceptor/chemoreceptor afferents
Damage to Reticular Activating System produces irreversible coma
Traversed by basilar artery and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
parts.histology: Complex mosaic of white matter longitudinal tracts interspersed with reticular formation multi-dendritic neuron networks and cranial nerve motor/sensory nuclei.

quizBank.prompt: What arterial anastomosis ensures collateral circulation to the brain?
quizBank.rationale: The Circle of Willis interconnects the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems at the base of the brain.
